title: MATKP Mini-Review: Aging
bodyHtml:
Aging is associated with profound and detrimental changes in adipose tissue physiology. These include reduced mitochondrial function, altered adipokine secretion (often leading to a pro-inflammatory profile), and a notable adipose depot redistribution of fat—specifically, an accumulation of visceral fat coupled with a loss of subcutaneous fat. Aging also blunts critical metabolic responses, such as lipolysis and thermogenesis [Tchkonia et al., 2010].

Comparative biology offers unique insights into aging resilience. Long-lived mammals, such as naked mole-rats, demonstrate remarkable preservation of adipose tissue function and immune tolerance with age, contrasting sharply with shorter-lived rodents. Emerging comparative data suggest that longevity correlates with reduced visceral fat accumulation and improved immune profiles within adipose tissue [Buffenstein, 2008]. Understanding these interspecies differences may reveal novel targets for promoting healthy adipose aging.

While rodent models provide critical mechanistic insights into adipose aging, they may not fully recapitulate the complex patterns observed in human aging. For instance, many rodent studies focus on early and late age comparisons, often lacking critical middle-aged timepoints, and historically, most have focused predominantly on male subjects. High-resolution techniques like single-cell sequencing and depot-specific longitudinal studies are still rare outside of mouse models, and we currently lack detailed maps of cellular senescence across adipose depots and mammalian species. There is a critical need for comprehensive longitudinal and multi-omic datasets in larger mammals, spanning developmental to geriatric stages, to capture depot-specific gene expression, immune cell profiles, and metabolic fluxes. Such data will significantly enhance our understanding of adipose aging in clinically relevant contexts.

Key References:

Tchkonia T, et al. (2010). Nature Reviews Endocrinology, 6(2):87–98.

Buffenstein R. (2008). Exp Gerontol, 43(1):10–4.
